claim: Crows that learned the trap-tube kept avoiding the trap after arbitrary cues were removed (3 of 3 passed transfers 1-2) and solved a visually different trap-table at first trial (3 of 3). Only 3 of 6 crows learned the tube at all.
agent_test: Same-lab sources only (Taylor 2009, Taylor 2020, Taylor/Roberts 2009 follow-up). Treat as single-lab until an outside lab replicates. Test: after our agent solves a task with arbitrary cues, remove each cue and re-ask on a surface-different but structure-equal task; score first-trial correct.

claim: Passing the cue-removal and trap-table transfers did not extend to the two-hole transfer where one hole had a base: all 3 crows failed (binomial p=0.0156 for the worst-pattern result). The skill is avoiding the visible hole, not a general rule about support.
agent_test: Include a transfer item that keeps the look but changes the causal feature (a decoy). Pass only if the agent fails the decoy less than a cue-matching baseline at equal tokens.
audit: downgraded 2026-10-31 by check_established.py: only 1 opened source(s) from distinct authors

claim: Taylor himself (2020) reads the crow result as knowledge of observable features only, not unobservable forces. Crows showed no preference for heavy over light stones (Neilands 2016, second-hand).
agent_test: Do not claim causal reasoning from one transfer pass; report which causal feature was varied.

claim: Great apes learn trap-tube and trap-platform but performance on the two is uncorrelated (r=0.13, p=0.57, N=20); first trials were not above chance (platform 14/20, tube 12/20). So no evidence of transfer between functionally equal tasks.
agent_test: Same paper read by two agents (not independent). Test: correlate agent success on two surface-different tasks with the same structure; low correlation suggests cue learning.

claim: Ape failures on trap tasks are partly caused by tool-use load and action constraints: apes preferred raking over pushing (64.5% vs 18% of pretest strategies, Martin-Ordas et al. 2008), around 80% of 37 apes solved the trap-table on trial 1 when they could choose where to insert a single tool (Girndt et al. 2008), and apes using fingers in a maze outperformed apes using a stick (Voelter and Call 2014).
agent_test: A failed transfer can be an interface cost. Re-run failed transfers with a simplified action format and see if the pass rate rises.
audit_note: The '20 of 24 apes' trial-1 figure is in none of the listed evidence; the only matching source (Girndt et al. 2008) reports 'around 80%' of 37 apes solving on trial 1 when they chose where to insert a single tool; the capuchin part is unsupported by the opened sources.
claim_before_audit: Ape and capuchin failures on trap tasks are partly caused by tool-use load and action constraints: raking beat pushing (64.5% vs 18% in one pretest), 20 of 24 apes avoided the trap on trial 1 with one tool, and finger mazes beat stick mazes.

claim: Adult humans also fail the inverted-trap control (insert at far end, 52/60 in Exp 1; 40/40 with effective trap), so passing that control is not required to show causal understanding.
agent_test: c02 only repeats a08 second-hand. Do not make one control the only test; use two or more triangulating controls.

claim: Trap-tube evidence rests on tiny samples: across 116 comparative physical-cognition experiments the median N is 7, 15 of 87 had zero passers, median passers 3; 44-59% of papers claimed positive results.
agent_test: Report agent transfer results over many items and seeds with intervals, not one or three runs.

claim: Corvid Aesop's-fable results are split: crows pass water vs sand (76.3%), sinking vs floating (88.0%), solid vs hollow (89.0%), but fail narrow vs wide (39.3% to narrow) and the U-tube. A pooled analysis reads this as learning from successful drops with no transfer across tasks.
agent_test: Compare first-trial choice with the trial-by-trial learning curve: accuracy that comes from learning inside the task is not transfer.

claim: Animal-AI Testbed: children (6-10) beat 2019-style RL agents on animal-cognition tasks (mean 0.605 vs 0.341); on average 0% of agents passed causal levels 3, 6, 8, 9, 10. Dreamer-v3 beat random by 6.5x vs 47x for children.
agent_test: Run the Animal-AI trap-tube items against our scaffold vs plain model at equal tokens.
audit_note: All four listed lines come from one lab (Voudouris/Crosby/Cheke/Halina group): a16 and c01 are the same 2022 paper, and the 2024 Animal-AI Environment paper is a follow-up by overlapping authors; numbers themselves match (0.6052 vs 0.3412, 0% at L3/6/8/9/10, Dreamer-v3 odds ratio 6.54 vs children 47.2, which are odds of passing vs random, not score multiples).

claim: LLMs without tuning (Claude 3.5 Sonnet, GPT-4o, Gemini 1.5 Pro) controlling an Animal-AI agent did some level 1-2 tasks and only sporadic level 5, 6, 8 tasks, below children. One in-context expert example gave no reliable help.
agent_test: All lines come from one paper. Controls were coarse and 12 trials per level. Re-run with newer models and a finer action interface.

claim: No published test gives an LLM the crow trap-tube, trap-table or Aesop's fable task directly (negative search, 2026-10-31).
agent_test: A gap and a chance: build a text or grid trap-tube with cue-removal and decoy transfers.

claim: LLM performance drops on counterfactual variants of familiar tasks: in letter-string analogies GPT models fall from the standard alphabet to permuted and symbol alphabets while humans stay roughly constant (pooled over all alphabets, humans 0.753 vs GPT-3 0.488, GPT-3.5 0.350, GPT-4 0.452; Lewis and Mitchell 2024), and in Wu et al. 2024 counterfactual performance is above random for most of 11 tasks but lower than default for all. Calling this the LLM version of the cue-removal test is an interpretation.
agent_test: Standard G3 check: swap the surface (alphabet, symbols, base) and see if accuracy holds, for our scaffold at equal tokens.
audit_note: The pooled letter-string accuracies (humans 0.753; GPT-3 0.488, GPT-3.5 0.350, GPT-4 0.452) are averaged over all alphabets including the standard-order one, so they show a human-LLM gap, not the drop itself; the drop for GPT models going from standard to permuted/symbol alphabets (humans staying roughly constant) is in Lewis and Mitchell's per-alphabet figures.
claim_before_audit: LLM performance drops on counterfactual variants of familiar tasks with the same abstract structure: letter-string analogies (humans 0.753; GPT-3 0.488, GPT-3.5 0.350, GPT-4 0.452 pooled) and 11 tasks in Wu et al.; humans stay level. This is the LLM version of the cue-removal test.

claim: Vision-language models only partly handle intuitive-physics and causal tasks: above chance on 2 of 3 tasks but below humans; fine-tuning on towers helps in-domain (including taller towers) but not on counterfactual stability.
agent_test: Small gains from tuning do not transfer across causal domains. Test the scaffold on both tower and Michotte-style items.
audit_note: Both supporting papers (2311.16093 and 2502.15678) are by the same first author and lab (Schulze Buschoff, Schulz); also 'above chance on 2 of 3 tasks' holds only for the largest models (GPT-4, Claude-3 Opus), which the claim does not say. Fine-tuning findings do match.

claim: On Pearl-ladder text questions, base models are near chance; GPT-4 reaches 62.03% and CausalCoT 70.40% (rungs 83.35 / 67.47 / 62.05). Accuracy falls from rung 1 to rung 3.
agent_test: Same paper read twice; the values were re-checked against the arXiv text this pass. Compare to plain prompting at equal tokens, since CausalCoT uses extra tokens.

claim: Pure causal inference from correlation statements (Corr2Cause) is close to random for 17 LLMs (best F1 33.38, BART MNLI; GPT-4 29.08; random uniform 20.38), and fine-tuned models lose drastically on perturbed test sets (F1 drops of up to 39.29 points on the paraphrased set and up to 62.30 after variable refactorization). A structured graph-first prompt lifted Qwen3-32B F1 from 32.71 to 48.26 (Sun et al. 2025).
agent_test: Test a build-the-graph-first step vs direct answer at equal tokens on a perturbed set.
audit_note: Jin et al. say fine-tuned models 'drop drastically, by up to 39.29' F1 points on the paraphrased set (and up to 62.30 after variable refactorization); the claim turns the size of the drop into a score ('as low as 39.29').
claim_before_audit: Pure causal inference from correlation statements (Corr2Cause) is near random for 17 LLMs (best F1 33.38) and fine-tuned models collapse on paraphrased or variable-renamed sets (as low as 39.29). A graph-first prompt lifted Qwen3-32B F1 from 32.71 to 48.26.

claim: Where models score high on text causal tasks (Tubingen pairs 97%, counterfactual 92%, actual causality 86%; new post-cutoff pairs 80.3% GPT-3.5 and 98.5% GPT-4), the tasks lean on retrieved knowledge, not discovery from scratch.
agent_test: Use post-cutoff or invented-entity variants to separate memory from reasoning.

claim: In blicket-style active causal discovery, LM agents infer OR rules but fail on equally evidenced AND rules (disjunctive bias), worse from 4 to 8 objects. Test-time hypothesis sampling removes the deficit. A 2026 study finds adults do well on AND rules only with free interventions.
agent_test: Check our agent on AND rules at 4 and 8 objects; add a sample-many-hypotheses-then-pick-most-informative-action step and test at equal tokens.
audit_note: The LM-agent finding (GX-Chen et al. 2025) and the adult study (Samiei et al. 2026) are by an overlapping team (GX-Chen, Lin, Richards, Precup, Yiu, Gopnik), and c15/c16 are one paper; also 'removes the deficit' and 'only with free interventions' go beyond 'no decrease in conjunctive vs disjunctive' and 'active exploration substantially improves' conjunctive reasoning.

claim: Children and LLMs diverge on causal over-hypotheses, but results are mixed: LaMDA scored lowest on the causal domain (1.34 vs 2.91 perception) while text LLMs matched children on association-based tool choice.
agent_test: Mixed evidence (c07 near-human tool choice with older models; c09 a causal deficit). Test tool-innovation items with unrelated-but-functional objects.

claim: Scaffolds help reasoning but can hurt raw output: a context-graph state machine raised reasoning-eligible accuracy on shifting-rule blicket from 73.3% to 93.9% (p=0.038), while raw accuracy got worse without dynamic behaviours. Vendor preprint.
agent_test: Replicate with an independent model family before using.

claim: Longer reasoning or more history does not reliably help in animal-style tasks: in CheeseBench, CoT scored 31.9% vs default 46.7%, and history 10 scored 26.7% vs 57.0% for history 1.
agent_test: Check whether our scaffold hurts on grid-world causal tasks at equal tokens.

claim: A hypothesis-proposing LLM plus code execution and information-gain experiment selection tracks human behaviour on rule discovery (R2 up to .57) better than direct ReAct play.
agent_test: Ablate explicit hypotheses and online updating on a rule task.

claim: Outside-lab trap-tube and related trap-task studies find that few animals pass and almost none transfer: 3 of 7 rooks passed the modified trap-tube and 0 passed transfer; Darwin's finches 0 transfers (2 non-tool-using woodpecker finches solved the initial task); hooded crows: 1 of 6 avoided the trap on trial 1 and 4 learned by trial and error; in a related tray/gap task only 1 of 8 macaws and caiques showed clear transfer; zebra finches (N=34) were at chance on a trap-gap transfer test; no pet dog (25) reached 60% correct on the trap tube. We did not find a replication of the full Taylor 2009 series, but that absence is not demonstrated by these sources.
agent_test: Report 'passed training' and 'passed transfer' as separate rates. Expect transfer to be rare even when training is common.
audit_note: Per-species counts check out (rooks 3/7 and 0 transfers, finches 0 transfers, crows 1/6 first trial and 4 by trial and error, 1 of 8 parrots clear transfer, no dog reached 60%), but the zebra-finch study is a trap-gap task and the parrot study a tray/gap task, not trap-tube work, and the 'no outside lab has reproduced the full Taylor 2009 series' negative is not shown by any listed source.
claim_before_audit: No outside lab has reproduced the full Taylor 2009 series (cue removal, two-hole decoy, trap-table) with first-trial data. Outside-lab trap-tube work finds that some birds learn the tube and none or almost none transfer: rooks 3 of 7 passed, 0 transferred; Darwin's finches 0 transfers; hooded crows 1 of 6 passed on trial 1, 4 by trial and error; macaws and caiques 1 of 8 clear transfer; zebra finches (N=34) transfer at chance; dogs (25) never reached 60%.

claim: The 14-crow follow-up is confirmed from the full text: 8 naive crows were at chance on the trap-table, and only the 3 that had solved the trap-tube passed; an inverted two-trap tube showed no spatial-rule preference. Still the same lab as the 2009 paper.
agent_test: Include a naive control run (no source-task training) on the transfer item; it must score at chance.

claim: Aesop's fable passes are mostly learning inside the task, not a first-trial edge. Re-analysis of 33 tasks with 28 birds: water-vs-sand and float-vs-sink show no first-trial preference (OR 0.53 and 1.23) but a learning slope (OR 1.04 and 1.05 per insertion, both p<.001); hollow-vs-solid has a strong first-trial preference for solid (OR 57.02) and no learning. No transfer between tasks (OR 0.81, p=.22). Ghirlanda and Lind (36 birds, 23,928 choices) reach the same view: trial-and-error learning explains all 11 apparent successes.
agent_test: Fit first-trial accuracy and learning slope separately for any agent run; credit only the first-trial part as transfer.
audit_note: Hennefield's 0.81 (p=.22) is a task-order coefficient, read as 'no transfer'; 11 of 33 experiments in Ghirlanda and Lind rests on a secondary summary; otherwise numbers match.

claim: Failure on an inverted or ineffective-trap control does not show a lack of causal knowledge. Adults avoid functional traps 40/40 and 10/10 but push into the far end of a tube with an ineffective trap on 36 of 40 trials, and 15 to 16 of 19 avoid a hole that cannot trap, giving a causal reason. A fair pass rule is correct behaviour on functional configurations plus a written reason that names the causal feature, not a perfect score on ineffective-trap items.
agent_test: For an LLM agent, require correct choices on functional items and a stated causal reason; count the decoy as a separate bias check.

claim: Mecattaf 2024 gives per-level proportions only (n=12 trials per level, three 2024 models) with no per-task trap-tube result and no scaffold-vs-plain comparison; one in-context example gave mixed changes by model and level. Its child baseline is stated as 59 children, which is the number who completed all 40 tasks in Voudouris 2022; that paper analysed 52 after excluding 7 who failed Level-1 checks (44 after outlier removal in some contrasts).
agent_test: Do not quote a trap-tube result for LLMs from this paper. Quote 52 (Voudouris) or 59 (Mecattaf) with the source named.
audit_note: The 59 vs 52 child counts are not a real disagreement: Voudouris 2022 states 59 children completed all 40 tasks and 52 remained after excluding 7 who failed 2 of 4 Level-1 tasks (44 after the separate outlier rule); Mecattaf cites the pre-exclusion 59.
claim_before_audit: Mecattaf 2024 gives no per-task trap-tube result and no scaffold-vs-plain comparison. It reports per-level proportions only (n=12 trials per level, three 2024 models). One in-context example gave mixed changes. The child baseline is 59 children in Mecattaf and 52 analysed children (44 after outlier removal) in Voudouris 2022; the two papers disagree.

claim: Whether chain-of-thought helps or hurts depends on the task shape. It helped when it was a fixed procedure over a stated problem (CLadder: +8.37 on v1.5 but only +2.36 on v1.0; +9.65 on anti-commonsense stories; only +1.5 at rung 3). It hurt in sequential exploration with a small model and short context (CheeseBench Qwen2.5-VL-7B: CoT 31.9% vs default 46.7%, with 15 trials per cell and about +-25pp noise). No study tests CoT at equal tokens on a cue-removal transfer task.
agent_test: Compare plain, CoT and scaffold at equal total tokens on the same transfer items; do not adopt CoT or ban it on the strength of either paper.

claim: Current reasoning models narrow but do not remove the blicket AND deficit: gpt-5 and deepseek-reasoner are near-perfect on the OR rule, while AND stays harder and less efficient than top humans. Exact per-model AND values were not readable. No equal-token test of hypothesis sampling on these models exists.
agent_test: Run AND vs OR items on the target model, with and without code-held hypothesis sampling, at equal tokens.

claim: The action interface alone moves agent scores a lot. CheeseBench: one model ranged from 20% to 57% by history length and action batch size alone (k=4 51.9% vs k=16 20.0%). Matched MCP vs CLI interfaces diverge in 94.3% of 2,004 paired episodes, and a repair that fixes only interface wording gained up to 9.0 points. So a failed transfer item should be re-run with a simplified interface before it is read as missing causal knowledge. Apes show the same effect (raking 64.5% vs pushing 18%).
agent_test: Re-run each failed transfer item with the simplest action format; report both pass rates.
audit_note: CheeseBench values are from 15 trials per environment and the authors call them directional/noisy; the 64.5% vs 18% ape figure is a strategy-preference share in a pretest, not accuracy.
